title: Mentorship
text:
Mentorship is one of the most meaningful parts of my academic work.
I view doctoral mentorship as more than guiding a student toward the completion of a dissertation. My goal is to help emerging scholars develop the critical thinking, methodological judgment, intellectual independence, and scholarly confidence needed to conduct rigorous research and contribute meaningfully to their fields.
My approach combines high expectations with developmental support. I encourage students to ask difficult questions, challenge their assumptions, defend their methodological choices, and continuously strengthen the alignment and contribution of their research.

The goal is not simply to complete a dissertation. The goal is to develop an independent scholar.





I approach doctoral mentorship through several guiding principles.


Strong research begins with a meaningful problem.
Before selecting a methodology or analytical technique, I encourage doctoral researchers to clearly articulate:

What problem exists?
Who is affected by the problem?
Why does the problem matter?
What is already known?
What remains unknown?
Why is additional research needed?

A sophisticated analytical method cannot compensate for a poorly defined research problem.




One of the most important principles I emphasize is alignment across the study.
A well-designed dissertation should demonstrate a clear connection among:

Problem → Purpose → Theory → Research Questions → Hypotheses → Data → Methodology → Evidence → Contribution

When these elements are aligned, the research tells a coherent story.
When they are not aligned, even technically sophisticated research can become difficult to defend or interpret.
I work with doctoral researchers to continually evaluate this alignment throughout the dissertation process.




I encourage students to resist choosing a statistical method simply because it is familiar, popular, or advanced.
Instead, we ask:

What does the research question require?
What type of data are available?
What assumptions must be satisfied?
What alternative methods could be considered?
What can the analysis legitimately tell us?
What can it not tell us?

The objective is not to use the most complicated method.
The objective is to use the most appropriate method to answer the research question rigorously.





Depending on the research problem, I mentor doctoral researchers using a range of quantitative and analytical approaches.




Research design
Survey research
Secondary data analysis
Measurement
Hypothesis testing
Regression modeling





Structural equation modeling
Latent variable modeling
Bayesian methods
Predictive analytics
Machine learning
Multivariate analysis





Systematic literature reviews
Meta-analysis
Bibliometric analysis
Science mapping
Evidence synthesis
Reproducible reviews







Although every dissertation is different, I view doctoral research as an iterative process of refinement.


The researcher identifies a meaningful and researchable problem supported by evidence.



The literature is critically examined to determine what remains unknown, unresolved, or insufficiently understood.



The study clearly articulates what it intends to investigate and why.



The researcher identifies theories or conceptual frameworks that explain the relationships being investigated.



Research questions emerge logically from the problem, purpose, literature, and theoretical framework.



The research design, data, measures, and analytical methods are selected to appropriately address the research questions.



The researcher conducts the analysis while evaluating assumptions, uncertainty, robustness, and alternative explanations.



Results are interpreted in relation to theory, prior research, limitations, and the context of the study.



The researcher explains how the study contributes to scholarship, practice, methodology, or future research.



Whenever appropriate, I encourage students to move beyond the dissertation by presenting their work at conferences and developing manuscripts for publication.





My feedback is designed to help students think more deeply about their research.
Rather than simply telling a researcher what to change, I often use questions such as:

What evidence supports this claim?


How does this connect to your research problem?


What is the theoretical justification for this relationship?


Does this research question require the data you plan to collect?


What alternative explanation should you consider?


What would a skeptical reviewer ask here?


What is genuinely new about this study?


What can you conclude from these results, and what can you not conclude?

These questions are intended to help doctoral researchers develop the ability to critically evaluate their own work.
Over time, the goal is for students to begin asking these questions themselves.




A successful dissertation is an important milestone, but I encourage students to think beyond the dissertation itself.
Doctoral research can become the foundation for:

Peer-reviewed journal articles
Conference presentations
Professional presentations
Research collaborations
Open-source analytical projects
Future research studies
Organizational or policy impact
Continued scholarly development

Whenever appropriate, I encourage doctoral researchers to identify opportunities to extend their dissertation into a broader program of scholarship.




I increasingly encourage doctoral researchers to incorporate reproducible research practices into their work.
Depending on the study, this may include:

Clear documentation of analytical decisions
Organized project structures
Version control
Reproducible analytical code
Transparent data preparation
Research protocols
Pre-registration
Sensitivity and robustness analyses
Open Science Framework documentation
GitHub repositories
Quarto research reports

The goal is to help researchers develop practices that strengthen transparency and make their work easier to understand, evaluate, and extend.




Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing how researchers search literature, write code, analyze data, and communicate scholarly ideas.
I encourage doctoral researchers to develop the judgment needed to use these tools responsibly.
AI can support aspects of the research process, but researchers remain responsible for:

Verifying information
Evaluating evidence
Protecting confidential and sensitive data
Identifying potential bias
Understanding analytical methods
Checking AI-generated code
Maintaining appropriate attribution
Following institutional and publication policies
Taking intellectual ownership of the final research

Human judgment remains central to rigorous scholarship.




The emerging INSIGHT Lab is envisioned as an extension of this mentorship philosophy.
As the research community develops, doctoral students and graduate researchers may have opportunities to participate in collaborative projects involving:

Artificial intelligence
Data science
Health analytics
Education and learning analytics
Advanced quantitative methods
Meta-analysis
Bibliometric research
Reproducible research

The goal is to create opportunities for students to experience research as a collaborative scholarly process, not only as an individual dissertation requirement.




One of the most rewarding aspects of mentorship is seeing students develop confidence in their ability to contribute new knowledge.
I am particularly proud when students move from asking:

“What do I need to do to finish my dissertation?”

toward asking:

“What does the evidence tell us, and what should we investigate next?”

That transition represents an important step in developing a scholarly identity.
As this site grows, this section will highlight selected student accomplishments, including:

Dissertation proposal milestones
Successful dissertation defenses
Conference presentations
Peer-reviewed publications
Research collaborations
Awards and recognitions







Dissertation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Impact of Leader-Member Exchange (LMX) Quality on Employee Turnover Intentions
Dr. Shemika S. Miller completed her doctoral dissertation at Northwood University in 2024. Her research used systematic review and meta-analytic methods to synthesize evidence on the relationship between leader-member exchange quality and employee turnover intentions.
I had the privilege of serving as her dissertation chair and supporting her through the research process, including the development of the study, methodological decisions, quantitative synthesis, interpretation of findings, and successful completion of the dissertation.
Her work represents the type of doctoral scholarship I aim to encourage: research that is theoretically grounded, methodologically rigorous, evidence-based, and positioned to contribute to both scholarship and organizational practice.

View the Dissertation on ProQuest





As my mentorship portfolio continues to grow, I hope to use this space to celebrate doctoral researchers and alumni whose work contributes meaningful knowledge to their fields.
Future scholar profiles may highlight:

Dissertation research
Successful defenses
Peer-reviewed publications
Conference presentations
Awards and recognitions
Collaborative research
Continued scholarly contributions

My goal is to recognize not only the completion of the doctoral journey, but also the continued development of researchers as independent scholars and contributors to their professional communities.



I am interested in mentoring and collaborating on research that intersects with my broader research program, particularly in:

Artificial intelligence and human decision-making
AI adoption and attitudes
Data science and predictive analytics
Health and wellness analytics
Education and learning analytics
Structural equation modeling
Bayesian methods
Meta-analysis and research synthesis
Bibliometric analysis
Reproducible research

Prospective research collaborations should align with principles of methodological rigor, intellectual curiosity, transparency, and meaningful scholarly contribution.




My responsibility as a mentor is to support students while also challenging them to produce their strongest work.
I strive to create a mentorship environment characterized by:
Rigor — Research claims should be supported by appropriate evidence.
Alignment — Every component of the study should contribute to answering the research questions.
Curiosity — Researchers should remain open to unexpected findings and alternative explanations.
Independence — Students should develop confidence in making and defending scholarly decisions.
Integrity — Research should be conducted transparently, responsibly, and ethically.
Growth — Feedback should be viewed as an opportunity to strengthen both the research and the researcher.
Ultimately, I hope the researchers I mentor leave the doctoral process not only with a completed dissertation, but with the confidence and skills to continue asking important questions and contributing meaningful knowledge.

title: Teaching
text:
My teaching philosophy is grounded in the belief that students learn best when they can connect theory, analytical reasoning, practical application, and reflection.
I aim to create learning environments where students do more than use analytical tools. I want them to understand why a method is appropriate, how to evaluate evidence critically, how to communicate findings clearly, and how to make responsible decisions with data and artificial intelligence.
My teaching interests span data science, artificial intelligence, analytics, research methods, advanced quantitative methods, and doctoral education.






This research-centered seminar examines current scholarship in machine learning and predictive artificial intelligence.
Students engage with scholarly literature, evaluate emerging methods, lead discussions, and develop their ability to communicate research critically and clearly.
Topics may include:

Machine learning research
Predictive modeling
Neural networks
Reinforcement learning
Experimental methods in machine learning
Computational learning theory
Evolutionary computation
Emerging AI methods
Research communication
Reproducible analytical workflows

The course also introduces students to tools and practices that support modern analytical research, including Python, R, Power BI, GitHub, and Quarto, where appropriate.
A central goal of the course is to help students move from being consumers of AI tools toward becoming thoughtful researchers who can critically evaluate, apply, and communicate developments in predictive artificial intelligence.

I approach teaching through four core principles.


Students learn analytical concepts more deeply when they apply them to authentic problems and real datasets.
Whenever possible, I use examples that require students to make decisions rather than simply calculate answers.



Technology changes quickly. Analytical reasoning remains essential.
I encourage students to ask:

What is the research or business question?
What type of data do we have?
What assumptions are being made?
Why is this method appropriate?
What does the result actually mean?
What alternative explanation might exist?

The goal is to ensure that students understand the reasoning behind an analysis rather than simply following a sequence of software commands.



Modern data science requires more than producing a final result.
Students should learn how to document their analytical decisions, organize code, use version control, and create workflows that others can understand and reproduce.
I increasingly incorporate tools such as GitHub and Quarto to help students develop these habits.



Artificial intelligence is becoming part of how students learn, analyze data, write code, and conduct research.
Rather than treating AI only as a prohibited tool or an automatic solution, I encourage students to develop the judgment needed to use AI responsibly.
Students should be able to:

Verify AI-generated information
Evaluate the quality of AI-generated code
Identify potential bias
Protect sensitive information
Document AI use where appropriate
Maintain intellectual ownership of their work
Recognize when human judgment is essential






My approach to teaching data science emphasizes the connection among:

Question → Data → Analysis → Evidence → Decision

Students should understand that a technically sophisticated model is not automatically a useful model.
I encourage them to consider:

Predictive performance
Interpretability
Generalizability
Bias and fairness
Practical relevance
Ethical consequences

In AI-focused courses, I also emphasize the distinction among different forms of artificial intelligence, including predictive, generative, and increasingly agentic systems.
The goal is to help students understand both what these systems can do and the conditions under which they should be trusted.




One area I am increasingly integrating into my teaching is reproducible analytical practice.
Students can use GitHub to:

Manage analytical projects
Track changes
Collaborate with others
Review contributions
Practice version control
Build a public portfolio

Students can use Quarto to:

Integrate narrative, code, and results
Create reproducible reports
Develop presentations
Build websites
Produce research documents

Together, these tools help students learn practices that extend beyond a single course and prepare them for collaborative research and professional data science environments.

Research & Reproducibility

I select tools based on the learning objective rather than teaching technology for its own sake.




I frequently use real or realistic datasets to help students connect analytical methods with practical decisions.
Examples may include:

Predicting student success
Evaluating health outcomes
Modeling customer behavior
Identifying risk
Comparing machine learning models
Evaluating classification thresholds
Investigating relationships among latent constructs
Examining uncertainty through Bayesian methods

These applications encourage students to consider not only whether a model works, but also whether it answers the right question.




Doctoral education requires a different type of teaching.
Rather than providing students with predetermined solutions, doctoral mentorship requires helping them develop the ability to:

Define important research problems
Identify meaningful gaps
Construct theoretical arguments
Develop aligned research questions
Select defensible methods
Interpret findings cautiously
Recognize limitations
Communicate scholarly contributions

My goal is to challenge doctoral researchers while also creating a supportive environment in which they can develop confidence and independence.

My research informs what I teach.
My teaching helps me identify new research questions.
My mentorship helps emerging scholars contribute new knowledge.
This connection is also central to the vision of the INSIGHT Lab, where students and researchers can engage in collaborative, interdisciplinary, and reproducible scholarship.

Artificial intelligence is increasingly shaping how people learn, work, communicate, and make decisions. My research in this area examines both the opportunities created by AI and the human, educational, and organizational factors that influence its effective use.

What factors influence people’s attitudes toward and adoption of artificial intelligence?

Who and what shape the intellectual structure of a research domain?

How can research synthesis become more transparent and reproducible?
How can artificial intelligence responsibly support literature discovery and evidence synthesis?
How will retrieval-augmented generation and agentic AI change scientific research?
What safeguards are needed when AI becomes increasingly integrated into research workflows?




Current work in this area includes research on the evolution of retrieval-augmented generation for large language models, human–AI decision-making, and the development of robust and reproducible bibliometric workflows.
I am particularly interested in integrating tools and data sources such as OpenAlex, Bibliometrix, VOSviewer, R, Python, GitHub, and Quarto to create transparent research pipelines that can be reused and extended by other researchers.
A longer-term direction of this work is to examine how AI agents and human researchers may collaborate across the research lifecycle, from literature discovery and hypothesis generation to analysis, reproducibility, and scholarly communication.

Although these four streams are presented separately, they are intentionally interconnected.
For example:

Research on AI in education requires understanding human behavior, learning, and responsible technology adoption.
Research on health analytics benefits from advanced statistical methods and interpretable predictive models.
Research on human–AI decision-making connects artificial intelligence with psychology, organizations, health, and education.
Research on bibliometrics and meta-analysis strengthens our ability to understand accumulated scientific evidence.
Research on reproducibility and emerging AI influences how scholarship across all of these areas is conducted.

Together, these streams form a broader research agenda focused on the responsible use of data, intelligence, and evidence to understand complex systems and improve human outcomes.

Complex problems often require perspectives and methods from multiple disciplines.



Research questions, theory, data, and analytical methods should be carefully aligned.



Research workflows should be transparent and reproducible whenever possible.



Technological innovation should be evaluated in relation to the people, communities, and systems it affects.



Research is strengthened through collaboration, transparency, and the responsible sharing of knowledge.



Developing the next generation of researchers is an important part of scholarly impact.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models
text:
Bibliometrics Artificial Intelligence Open Science
Status: Ongoing Research
Research Stream: Science of Research & Emerging AI
Methods: Bibliometric Analysis · Science Mapping · Computational Text Analysis




Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has emerged as an important approach for extending the capabilities of large language models by integrating information retrieval with generative artificial intelligence.
As research in this area expands rapidly, there is a need to systematically examine how the field has developed, who and what have shaped its intellectual structure, and which themes are emerging.
This project uses bibliometric analysis and science mapping to examine the evolution of research on retrieval-augmented generation for large language models.
The study is designed not only to describe publication growth, but also to investigate the intellectual, conceptual, and collaborative structures shaping the field.




The primary unit of analysis is:

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for Large Language Models (LLMs)

This scope intentionally focuses on the modern RAG paradigm associated with large language models rather than broadly combining it with earlier retrieval-based generation approaches in traditional natural language processing.
Earlier retrieval-generation methods may provide important historical context, but they are conceptually distinguished from the primary unit of analysis.
The current study period focuses on research published through 2025, allowing the analysis to examine the emergence and rapid growth of the field while using a complete publication year as the endpoint.




The project is guided by the following broad research questions:


How has scholarly research on retrieval-augmented generation for large language models evolved over time?



Who are the most influential authors, institutions, countries, publications, and sources contributing to RAG research?



What patterns of collaboration characterize the global RAG research community?



What citation and knowledge structures define the intellectual foundations of RAG research?



What major themes, research clusters, and emerging topics characterize the development of RAG for large language models?





A central methodological consideration in this project is how to identify relevant RAG research comprehensively.
Searching only for the exact phrase “retrieval-augmented generation” may exclude relevant studies that describe similar architectures, approaches, or mechanisms using different terminology.
The project therefore uses a broader metadata-based retrieval strategy.
Records are retrieved using relevant information available through:

Titles
Abstracts
Keywords
Concepts and topics
Related metadata fields

The search incorporates a comprehensive set of terms associated with retrieval-augmented generation and large language models.
Retrieved records are subsequently screened for relevance according to predefined eligibility criteria.
This approach is designed to improve recall while reducing unnecessary selection bias introduced by relying on a single exact phrase.






The primary bibliographic data source for this project is OpenAlex.
OpenAlex provides open scholarly metadata that can support:

Publication retrieval
Author analysis
Institutional analysis
Country-level analysis
Citation analysis
Topic and concept analysis
Collaboration networks

The use of an open bibliographic data source also aligns with the project’s broader commitment to reproducible and transparent research.





The project follows a reproducible bibliometric workflow:

Define Scope → Develop Search Strategy → Retrieve Records → Screen for Relevance → Clean Metadata → Analyze → Visualize → Interpret → Reproduce



Clearly define RAG for LLMs as the primary conceptual domain.



Construct a comprehensive metadata search strategy designed to balance precision and recall.



Retrieve scholarly metadata through OpenAlex.



Manually screen retrieved records using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria.



Address issues such as:

Duplicate records
Author name variants
Institutional name variants
Keyword inconsistencies
Missing metadata




Analyze publication growth, productivity, impact, collaboration, citation structures, and research themes.



Develop network-based representations of the field.



Use keyword analysis and computational text methods to identify developing research topics.



Maintain transparent documentation of search, screening, cleaning, and analytical decisions.





The project combines descriptive bibliometrics, network analysis, science mapping, and computational text analysis.


Potential indicators include:

Annual scientific production
Citation patterns
Most productive authors
Most influential authors
Leading institutions
Leading countries
Most influential publications
Most relevant publication sources




Collaboration networks may examine:

Author collaboration
Institutional collaboration
International collaboration




Citation-based analyses may include:

Co-citation analysis
Bibliographic coupling
Citation networks




The conceptual development of the field may be examined through:

Keyword co-occurrence
Thematic mapping
Thematic evolution
Topic analysis
Trend topics






In addition to traditional bibliometric methods, the project explores computational text analysis to identify meaningful terminology within the literature.


Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) may be used to identify terms that are particularly informative within documents or groups of documents.
This can complement author-provided keywords and bibliometric concept metadata by identifying terminology directly from titles and abstracts.
The integration of bibliometric and text-analytic approaches may provide a richer understanding of how RAG research themes have evolved.

title: About
text:
I am a data scientist, professor, researcher, academic leader, and doctoral mentor whose work sits at the intersection of data science, artificial intelligence, education, health analytics, and advanced quantitative methods.
I currently serve as an Associate Professor of Data Science and Analytics at Harrisburg University of Science and Technology, where my work focuses on teaching, research, doctoral mentorship, and the development of interdisciplinary scholarship in artificial intelligence and analytics.
My professional journey has moved across engineering, computer science, instructional technology, business analytics, and academic leadership. This interdisciplinary background shapes how I approach both research and teaching: I am interested not only in developing and applying sophisticated analytical methods, but also in understanding how data and technology can be used to improve human decision-making, learning, health, and organizational outcomes.


My academic training began in Electrical Engineering, with a concentration in computer and control engineering. I later earned a Master of Science in Computer Engineering, where my research focused on human–robot interaction and gesture imitation learning.
My interest in large-scale data and intelligent systems led me to pursue a Master of Science in Computer Science with a focus on big data analytics. My thesis examined unsupervised learning and image classification using high-performance computing clusters.
I subsequently earned a PhD in Instructional Design and Technology, where my dissertation examined factors predicting minority female students’ intentions to enroll in college STEM programs. This work deepened my interest in education, student success, learning analytics, and the role of data in understanding complex human outcomes.
My professional development has also included the Harvard Business Analytics Program, an Executive MBA from the Quantic School of Business and Technology, and advanced training in learning analytics and digital learning platforms.



My teaching philosophy is grounded in the belief that students learn best when they can connect theory, analytical reasoning, and practical application.
I have taught graduate and doctoral courses in analytics, artificial intelligence, machine learning, business decision-making, programming, SQL, research methods, and quantitative analysis. My teaching increasingly emphasizes reproducible research, critical thinking, responsible AI use, and the ability to translate analytical results into meaningful decisions.
At Harrisburg University, I am beginning a new chapter that includes teaching ANLY 735 – Research Seminar in Predictive AI and mentoring doctoral students through ANLY 799 – Doctoral Studies.
I am particularly interested in helping students move beyond learning analytical tools toward becoming thoughtful researchers and practitioners who can ask better questions, evaluate evidence critically, and communicate insights clearly.
Explore Teaching →



My scholarship is organized around four broad research streams:


I study how artificial intelligence, machine learning, and emerging technologies influence learning, decision-making, and human interaction. My interests include predictive AI, generative AI, agentic AI, AI literacy, human–AI collaboration, and attitudes toward artificial intelligence.



I use data science and advanced quantitative methods to investigate health and wellness outcomes, including sleep, physical activity, metabolic health, psychological wellness, epidemiology, and health informatics.



I am interested in applying and teaching rigorous analytical approaches including structural equation modeling, Bayesian statistics, machine learning, predictive modeling, meta-analysis, and multivariate methods.



I also study how research itself is conducted, synthesized, and communicated. My interests include bibliometrics, research synthesis, open science, reproducible workflows, retrieval-augmented generation, and emerging AI research methods.
Explore My Research →




My academic leadership experience includes curriculum development, program oversight, faculty mentorship, program assessment, enrollment and retention initiatives, and continuous improvement.
As a former Division Chair for graduate analytics and doctoral programs, I worked closely with faculty, administrators, and students to support curriculum quality, student success, faculty collaboration, and academic program development. I have also chaired doctoral dissertations and mentored students from proposal development through dissertation completion and scholarly dissemination.
I view academic leadership as an extension of teaching and mentorship. Effective leadership requires creating environments where faculty and students are supported, challenged, and empowered to grow.



Mentoring emerging scholars is one of the most meaningful parts of my academic work.
My approach to doctoral mentorship emphasizes:

Clear alignment among the research problem, purpose, questions, theory, and methodology
Rigorous and transparent research practices
Critical thinking and intellectual independence
Appropriate use of advanced analytical methods
Reproducibility and open science where appropriate
Research that makes both scholarly and practical contributions

I strive to help doctoral students move beyond completing a dissertation toward developing an identity as independent scholars.
Learn More About Mentorship →



One of my goals at Harrisburg University is to develop an interdisciplinary research community that connects data science, artificial intelligence, education, health, and advanced research methods.
The emerging INSIGHT Lab – Interdisciplinary Network for Science, Intelligence, Growth, Health & Technology – is envisioned as a collaborative space for faculty, doctoral students, graduate researchers, and external collaborators interested in using data and AI to address complex real-world problems.

Turning data into insight. Turning insight into impact.

Explore the INSIGHT Lab →



Outside of research and teaching, I enjoy activities that reinforce many of the same principles I value professionally: continuous learning, discipline, strategy, mentorship, and resilience.
I am an avid pickleball player and coach and also enjoy figure skating. These activities remind me that improvement is rarely linear and that meaningful progress often comes through practice, reflection, adaptation, and community.



As I begin this next chapter at Harrisburg University, my goal is to continue building a body of work that connects rigorous data science with meaningful human problems.
I am particularly interested in expanding interdisciplinary collaborations, mentoring emerging researchers, developing open and reproducible research workflows, and building the INSIGHT Lab into a community where students and scholars can pursue ambitious questions at the intersection of artificial intelligence, analytics, health, and education.
Ultimately, I hope my work contributes not only to better models and methods, but also to better decisions, stronger learning environments, healthier communities, and more thoughtful uses of technology.

I am interested in applying and teaching rigorous analytical approaches including structural equation modeling, Bayesian statistics, machine learning, predictive modeling, meta-analysis, and multivariate methods.



I also study how research itself is conducted, synthesized, and communicated. My interests include bibliometrics, research synthesis, open science, reproducible workflows, retrieval-augmented generation, and emerging AI research methods.

Our Mission
The mission of the INSIGHT Lab is to advance interdisciplinary research that connects data, artificial intelligence, and quantitative methods with meaningful human and societal challenges.
The lab seeks to:

Conduct rigorous and impactful interdisciplinary research
Advance responsible and human-centered applications of artificial intelligence
Develop reproducible and transparent research workflows
Support doctoral students and emerging researchers
Promote collaboration across disciplines, institutions, and sectors
Translate analytical findings into actionable knowledge
Create opportunities for students to participate in research, publication, and scholarly dissemination

title: INSIGHT Lab
text:
Research Pillars


Artificial Intelligence & Intelligent Systems
Research on predictive AI, generative AI, agentic AI, retrieval-augmented generation, human–AI collaboration, trust, explainability, responsible AI, and AI-supported decision-making.


Learning & Education Analytics
Research on AI literacy, learning analytics, student engagement, academic success, technology-enhanced learning, and responsible AI use in education.


Health & Wellness Analytics
Research applying data science and advanced analytics to sleep, physical activity, psychological wellness, population health, epidemiology, and health informatics.


Methods, Evidence & Open Science
Research advancing structural equation modeling, Bayesian methods, meta-analysis, bibliometrics, predictive modeling, reproducibility, and open science.

title: INSIGHT Lab
text:
Current and Emerging Research Directions
The INSIGHT Lab is designed to support a portfolio of interconnected research projects rather than a single narrow research agenda.
Current and emerging areas of interest include:

Human–AI Decision-Making
Examining how individuals and organizations interact with artificial intelligence when making decisions, including questions related to trust, explainability, uncertainty, accountability, and decision quality.


AI Attitudes and Adoption
Investigating the individual, psychological, organizational, and contextual factors that shape attitudes toward artificial intelligence and influence AI adoption.


Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Emerging AI
Studying the evolution, research landscape, applications, and methodological development of retrieval-augmented generation and other emerging AI systems.


Health and Wellness Analytics
Using public health and population datasets to investigate relationships among sleep, physical activity, psychological wellness, metabolic risk, and other health outcomes.


Reproducible Bibliometric Research
Developing transparent and reusable workflows that integrate tools such as OpenAlex, R, Bibliometrix, VOSviewer, and computational text analysis.


Research Synthesis and Meta-Analysis
Synthesizing evidence across studies to better understand complex relationships in artificial intelligence, education, health, and organizational research.

Advanced statistical modeling
Machine learning and AI research

Reproducible research workflows
Conference presentations

Open science and research dissemination

title: INSIGHT Lab
text:
A Reproducible Research Philosophy
The INSIGHT Lab is committed to research practices that make scholarship more transparent, reliable, and reusable.
Where appropriate, projects will emphasize:

Pre-registration of research questions and analytical plans
Transparent documentation of research decisions
Version control using Git and GitHub
Reproducible analytical workflows
Open-source statistical tools
Public code repositories
Open Science Framework project documentation
Clear reporting of methods and limitations
Responsible and transparent use of artificial intelligence

Research workflows may incorporate tools such as R, Python, Quarto, GitHub, JASP, Jamovi, Stata, SAS, Power BI, OpenAlex, Bibliometrix, and VOSviewer, depending on the needs of each project.
